title: Why Smart People Are Often So Bad at Changing Their Minds
author: Shane Snow
summary: Snow reports on his studies of businesspeople's intellectual humility and argues that what stops people changing their minds is belief, not intelligence or demographics. Respondents rated themselves highly in the abstract but did worse on scenario-based questions, and their beliefs about other people explained that gap far better than education or background. He links this to Nir Eyal's Beyond Belief and to team data showing that groups high in intellectual humility show more commitment, accountability and trust. The move is to turn a trait into a short list of four beliefs a leader can adopt and model. The piece closes by noting that adaptability also supports individual well-being.
points: Most people overrate how well they change their minds when tested on concrete scenarios.
Beliefs about others predict intellectual humility about ten times more than demographics do.
Believing that listening to bad ideas is a waste of time makes being wrong hurt more.
Teams with higher intellectual humility show more commitment, accountability and trust.
Four adoptable beliefs, such as curiosity over expertise, support changing one's mind.
quotes: Gender, education, where you grew up—all of those tended to correlate to people’s self-scores, but people’s beliefs affected scenario-based scores 10 times as much as their demographics.
People who believe that listening to people with bad ideas is “a waste of time” score lower on their own intellectual humility, and especially on the ability to separate your ego from your ideas.
People who believe that expertise is more important than curiosity score lower on intellectual humility and higher on overconfidence.

great leaders don’t just encourage people to develop the valuable skill of changing their minds; they reinforce it through everyday actions, rewarding openness rather than stubborn certainty or simply having the right answer.

teams where most of the members displayed higher intellectual humility showed dramatically higher levels of commitment to the team, accountability for their work and results, and trust among team members.
Belief 3: Being curious is more important than being the expert. Belief 4: Being able to change my mind is more valuable than being right.
